data.title: Unique Paths
data.summary:
Input: Two integers m and n representing the number of rows and columns of a grid.
Output: An integer representing the number of possible unique paths from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner, moving only down or right.
Rules: The robot can only move either down or right at any point in time.
constraints: The answer is guaranteed to be less than or equal to 2 * 10^9

data.key_insight: The number of ways to reach any cell (i, j) is the sum of the ways to reach the cell above it (i-1, j) and the cell to its left (i, j-1). We can optimize space from a 2D grid to a 1D array representing the current row.

steps.title: Initialize DP array
steps.detail: Create an array of size n filled with 1s, since there is only 1 way to reach any cell in the first row.

steps.title: Iterate through rows
steps.detail: For each row from the second to the m-th, update the DP array where each cell adds the value of the cell to its left.

steps.title: Return result
steps.detail: The last element of the DP array will contain the total unique paths to the bottom-right corner.

data.pattern_summary: Dynamic programming breaks a problem down into overlapping subproblems of the same type, storing the results of previous computations to avoid redundant work. Reach for it when counting combinations or finding optimal values where smaller sub-results combine to form larger ones.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic programming
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. The number of paths to any cell depends directly on the number of paths to its neighbors, and paths overlap across different branches.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers are used to scan linear structures from both ends or at different speeds, which does not map to traversing a 2D grid.

pattern_options.name: Greedy
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Greedy algorithms make locally optimal choices at each step without reconsidering, but here we need the total count of all valid path combinations.

pattern_options.name: Backtracking
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. While backtracking can explore every path, it lacks state reuse and leads to massive redundant calculations for grid traversal.

signals.hint: Implies we are counting all valid combinations rather than finding a single specific route.
Limits the directions of our transitions, meaning any cell (r, c) can only be reached from (r-1, c) or (r, c-1).

data.brute_force_idea: Use a recursive depth-first search function to explore every possible sequence of down and right moves from the top-left corner until reaching the bottom-right corner, summing up all successful arrivals.
data.brute_force_why: At every single cell, the algorithm branches into two recursive calls (down and right), creating an exponential decision tree.
data.bottleneck: The code repeatedly recalculates the number of paths from the same intermediate cells multiple times because it does not store results that have already been computed.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many times the function visits the exact same coordinates (r, c) across different branches of the recursive tree.
Notice that the path count for a cell depends only on its row and column indices, not on how you got there.
Consider what would happen if you saved the result of dfs(r, c) the first time you compute it so you never have to recompute it.

data.overview: The Unique Paths algorithm computes the number of paths from the top-left to the bottom-right corner of a grid using dynamic programming. By maintaining a 1D array, it iteratively accumulates the number of ways to reach each cell from the left and above.
data.intuition: Imagine walking through a city grid where every intersection has a sign telling you how many ways you could have possibly gotten there. Each step forward just adds the number of paths from your left neighbor to your current total.

flow_nodes.detail: Create a 1D array dp of size n filled with 1s.

flow_nodes.detail: Loop over each row from 1 to m-1.

flow_nodes.label: Next col?
flow_nodes.detail: Loop over each column from 1 to n-1.

flow_nodes.label: Update dp[j]
flow_nodes.detail: Add the value from the left cell: dp[j] += dp[j - 1].

flow_nodes.detail: Return the final value in the dp array.

pitfalls: Forgetting that the top row and left column only have 1 unique path.
Using a 2D array when O(n) space with a 1D array is sufficient.
Off-by-one errors in loop ranges for m and n.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force solution recomputes paths for the same grid cells repeatedly through recursive branching, leading to exponential time complexity. The optimized dynamic programming approach avoids this by building up the solution iteratively from the top-left to the bottom-right, storing only the necessary row states in a single 1D array.

derivation.note: Allocates and initializes the 1D array of size n once.
Loops m - 1 times over the rows.
Inner loop runs n - 1 times for each row.
Performs constant time addition and assignment per iteration.
Returns the last element of the array.

data.time_summary: The outer loop runs m times and the inner loop runs n times. Multiplying the loop bounds gives O(m * n) total time complexity, which is supported by the measured step growth.
data.space_summary: The space complexity is O(n) because the dp array maintains a fixed size equal to the number of columns n, reusing the same memory space across all rows.
data.takeaway: When a grid-based recursion re-visits the exact same subproblems, replace recursion with iterative dynamic programming and compress multi-dimensional state tables to lower space usage.
mistakes: Forgetting to initialize the 1D array values to 1, which causes path counts to compute incorrectly.
Using a 2D array when only the previous row's values are needed, wasting space.
Off-by-one errors in range bounds leading to missed cells or index out of range exceptions.
